---
title: "Introduction"
---
Multilevel models are a standard statistical tool for analyzing clustered data, which frequently occur in the social sciences (e.g., patients nested within therapists, students within classes, or employees within firms). In practice, such data sets are often characterized by a relatively small numbers of groups and by the presence of missing values.  
Methodological research has proposed a range of approaches to address each of these challenges separately. Small-sample corrections for multilevel models have been developed to improve statistical inference when the number of clusters is limited [@mcneishstaple14; @mcneish; @elff; @holtmann]. At the same time, modern missing-data methods have been extended to multilevel data structures [see e.g. @audigier; @endersupdate; @grundapa; @enders16; @yucel; @kahan].  
Some research has investigated how these two challenges interact, both for single-level regressions [see e.g. @mcneish17; @hippel] and in multilevel contexts [e.g., @mcneishgrowth; @shinshin; @shin; @zitzmann]. However, the existing literature remains limited, and many relevant scenarios have not yet been systematically investigated. 
Among these, situations in which predictor variables contain missing values and are simultaneously used to construct group-mean contextual effects represent one particularly important but understudied case.  
In applied research, effects at both the individual and the group level are often of interest and can be modeled within multilevel frameworks. Level-2 characteristics are frequently operationalized by aggregating Level-1 variables, resulting in so-called contextual effects [@snijders, p. 102; @luedtkecontext; @croon]. This approach is widely used in psychological research [e.g., @anderman; @sport]. At the same time, missing values in predictor variables pose additional challenges for statistical inference, as they complicate missing data handling compared to situations in which only the outcome variable is incomplete. Standard likelihood-based approaches such as full information maximum likelihood are not easily applicable in this setting.  
This thesis therefore investigates the suitability of modern approaches to handling missing data in small-sample multilevel models in which predictor variables are partially missing and simultaneously included as group-mean contextual predictors. Specifically, the performance of multiple imputation and fully Bayesian estimation is evaluated.  
The structure of this thesis is as follows: First, the theoretical foundations of multilevel models are introduced, and current methodological approaches for handling small samples and missing data are reviewed. Subsequently, a simulation study is conducted to investigate the performance of these methods under different data conditions.
